conversation.content: We're going to design a URL shortening service today, something like bit.ly. What questions do you have before we begin?
How many users do we expect?
About 100 million new URLs per day, with a 100:1 read-to-write ratio. What else would you like to know?
Do we need to support custom URLs?
Yes, custom aliases and auto-generated. URLs should have a configurable TTL. Do you want to do a capacity estimation before designing?
Sure. 100 million per day. That's... a lot of URLs. We'll need a big database for that.
Can you convert that to requests per second and estimate storage needs? That will help drive your design decisions.

Okay, 100 million divided by 86,400 seconds in a day... about 1,150 writes per second. With 100:1 ratio, that's 115,000 reads per second. For storage, if each URL is maybe 500 bytes, 100M times 500 bytes is 50 GB per day. Over a few years that adds up.
Good. Now walk me through the high-level architecture.

We'd have a web server that receives requests. For creating a short URL, the user sends the long URL and we generate a short code. We store the mapping in a database. For redirecting, the user hits the short URL and we look up the long URL and redirect them.
Can you be more specific? What kind of database? How do you generate the short code? How does the redirect work — what HTTP status code?
I'd use MySQL for the database. For the short code, we could hash the long URL with MD5 and take the first 7 characters. For the redirect, we return a 301.
Two issues there. First, MD5 of the long URL — what if two different long URLs produce the same first 7 characters? Second, you mentioned 301 — what's the implication for analytics?

Oh right, there could be collisions. We'd need to check if the short code already exists and if it does... try again? Maybe append a counter? And for 301 vs 302... I'm not sure what the difference is for analytics.

301 is permanent — browsers cache it and won't hit your server again, so you lose analytics on repeat visits. 302 is temporary — every request comes through your server. As for collision handling, appending a counter to an MD5 gets messy. Have you considered other approaches for generating unique codes?
We could use an auto-incrementing ID and convert it to base62. That way every ID is unique by definition.
Good. But with multiple app servers, how do you coordinate the auto-incrementing counter?
Um... we could use the database's auto-increment? MySQL can auto-increment on insert.
At 1,150 writes per second across multiple servers, using a single MySQL auto-increment becomes a bottleneck and single point of failure. How would you distribute ID generation?
We could have each server get a range of IDs. Like server 1 gets IDs 1-10000, server 2 gets 10001-20000, and so on. When a server runs out, it requests a new range from some central service.
Good. What about caching? 115K reads per second hitting the database directly won't work.
Right, we should add Redis as a cache. When a redirect request comes in, check Redis first. If it's there, redirect. If not, query MySQL, store in Redis, then redirect.
How much data would you cache? And what eviction policy?
Hmm, maybe cache everything? Or the most popular ones. I'd use LRU eviction so the least recently accessed ones get removed when we run out of memory.
Can you estimate the cache size? How much memory do you need for the hot set?
If 20% of URLs get most of the traffic, that's 20 million URLs per day. At 500 bytes each, that's 10GB. Redis can handle that easily on one machine.
What happens if the database grows to hundreds of billions of rows over time?
We'd need to shard the database. We could shard by the short code — hash it to determine which shard it goes to.
Alright, we're running low on time. Any final thoughts on the design?
I think the main components are the load balancer, app servers, Redis cache, and sharded MySQL. We'd also want rate limiting to prevent abuse and some monitoring.
Thanks for walking through the design. Appreciate your time.

strengths: Could do the math when prompted — capacity estimation was correct once guided
Arrived at reasonable solutions like range-based IDs and cache-aside pattern
Basic understanding of all major components
weaknesses: Never volunteered information — every design detail had to be pulled out by the interviewer
Initial approach with MD5 hashing showed lack of awareness of common pitfalls
No discussion of failure scenarios — what happens when cache or database goes down?
Didn't discuss 301 vs 302 trade-offs despite it being central to analytics requirement
Sharding answer was surface-level — no discussion of number of shards, rebalancing, or consistent hashing
Zero proactive thinking about edge cases or production concerns
